utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. First of all, we have to sit only with two Judges today because Judge Mindua is not available because of another urgent appointment, and therefore the Chamber decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Before the witness is being brought in I -- the Chamber wants to render an oral ruling on the Prosecution's motion for a rescission of protective measures for Witness 65 ter 200 which was made orally on the 30th of August, 2010. In order to properly deal with that, we should go for a short moment into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber finds that the requirements of Rule 75(J) have been satisfied, and thus grants the Prosecution's motion. The Chamber wishes to add one remark in this regard. As the parties must be aware, the witness number 200 is a 92 ter witness in that his testimony in the Krstic case was provisionally admitted into evidence by this Chamber's decision on the 30th of March this year. Since this witness gave evidence with a pseudonym and in closed session in that case, the transcripts, which is the witness's 92 ter evidence, remain under seal. Both parties should take into account the situation that this Chamber is not in a position to declassify these documents. Does any party want to raise something in this regard? Mr. Vanderpuye -- Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's my witness, and we will endeavour to get that record opened up. I don't think anyone will object, I don't think the witness will, so that our record is more open. So I think that's -- I hadn't remembered that particular problem, but I think that's probably what we'll do if -- if that's -- meets your approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber wanted to point out that there's a distinction between protective measures and confidentiality of documents, and therefore you should take the necessary steps in order to, yes, get the right things done. We still have to decide on the request of the Prosecution about the tendered documents. We will do that after the first break. The witness should be brought in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to say hello to all those present, also say hello to Ms. Frease. I wish that may there be peace in this house and may the divine providence bring justice not according to my wishes but according to God's will. At the beginning of today, since I was not able to do this last time because I had acceded the allotted time, I would like to apologise first of all to the interpreters because they had to work longer because of my question. Also, I would like to apologise to you because I was not precise in citing the documents that I was looking for in e-court, and I would like to apologise to the registry, the Prosecution, also to Mr. Vanderpuye, because I had compared him to a different Prosecutor from the Prosecutor's office, which of course cannot apply to him because he has always been fair to date. I would like to apologise to the Defence, because I also did not tell them in time what I would be using of the documents and in what manner I would be using them. Also, I would like to thank everybody, and perhaps we could work shorter if we're talking about the same team of terms. I'm willing to sacrifice some of my time in order to make up for what happened last Wednesday. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, thank you very much. I think everybody will appreciate your nice words. On the other hand, this is the normal procedure. These things happen. Don't worry about that, and I think the interpreters and the staff of the court are quite patient and they will assist us in future as well. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Frease, I also would like to apologise to you, because I quoted what was authentic as far as I was concerned, and that is what is stated in the video footage. However, as you saw, you didn't say that. So I apologise for putting the wrong quote attributing to you because I didn't have the transcript at my disposal. Hopefully today we will understand each other, and now I'm going to move to the questions that the Defence requires to put in these proceedings. Thank you very much. And I would like to apologise once again. My first question would be: We saw from the examination-in-chief that you have a Masters Degree in international relations. I would like to ask you if in your studies and later you acquired the knowledge necessary for the analysis of documents, including special training required in order to be able to analyse the documents at hand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct that I have a Masters Degree in international relations. I did not receive any specific training with respect to analysing radio intercepts. I would say that I have a -- that I pay a high degree of attention to detail in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you said in the examination-in-chief, you worked at the OTP at this Tribunal from April 1995 until July 2000, and then you were a special advisor of the OTP after that until the end of 2006, 2007. Please correct me if I didn't state everything correctly. My question is: The analysis of the material that refers to the intercepted communications from -- up to 1998, did you work on the analysis of this material for as long as you were at your post until 1998 and then 2000, and did you subsequently as a consultant or advisor also analyse these documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I worked on this material from about April of 1998 until I left the Tribunal in July of 2000, and then I worked on it again, as you say, from late 2006 until early 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for putting a long question to you. I'm interested in the second half of the question, the analysis of this material. Was that completed in the period from 1998 until 2000 when you were permanently employed at the Tribunal, or did you continue to do this analysis work later in your capacity as special advisor of the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued to do the analysis when I worked for the Tribunal from late 2006 until early 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, but for the transcript can you please tell us whether you were analysing the materials that you are testifying on now in these proceedings also? I know that you were working for the Tribunal then, but were you also doing an analysis of these materials that are the subject of your testimony now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you doing this work because you didn't have these materials available earlier but were receiving them successively, or was there some other reason that you did this analysis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't working for the Tribunal at the time, so I didn't have access to the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise. I think I misunderstood you. So from the year 2000 you did not work on the material that you are testifying about right now, yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 2000 and 2006 I did not work for the Tribunal. From 2000 -- late 2006, until early 2007, I did. At that time I had an opportunity to review material that had come in in the interim and to work on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether while you were working in this first period when you were still employed at the Tribunal and in this second period in your capacity as special advisor, did you at any point analyse any other documents, documents by any other army, for example the Croatian Army, the Muslim army, or any other party to the war also?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I analysed the material that had been -- that related to the Srebrenica investigation that had come to the Tribunal from the sources that we've discussed, namely from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the SDB from Tuzla. At that time, I did not look at any material from the Croatians or other transcripts from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether -- were you only dealing with the analysis of intelligence service or intelligence-type material such as the interception centre and the like? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you specify the period that you're talking about? Are you talking about my -- the entire time that I worked for the Tribunal or the latter period?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will repeat my question. I'm asking you whether in the period from 1998 to 2000 when you were working as an employee of the Tribunal you were engaged on the analysis of military intelligence material in this case by the services that were compiling secret data information by means of interception.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was working on that material, and I was also still very closely involved with the Srebrenica team, the investigative team. Early on I had participated in a lot of the field investigations. In the later period I worked primarily on the material that you mention, but again was always working with the investigative team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And other than yourself, was anybody else also tasked with analysing and processing communications that were received through the work of the Military Intelligence Service during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina other than your closest associates who were subordinated to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I believe that we were the only team in the Tribunal that had access to this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And you talked about the first time you went to the command of the 2nd Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina when you were given access to the intercepted communications tapes. My question is: Were you permitted to just see that these tapes existed, or did you also have the opportunity to acquaint yourself with the contents also? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were just given access to the material at that time without having access to reviewing it. That's my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when was the first time that you had the opportunity to review the material and look into the contents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have a specific type of material in -- in mind, whether the printouts, the notebooks, or the audio cassettes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the material in general, just like I said in my question, the material that you received from the Military Intelligence Service of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Perhaps -- when was the first time that you had the opportunity to review this material and find out its contents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in April I had a chance to -- well, I guess even in March when we first got the -- that binder, had an opportunity to look through it, the same for the notebooks in April, but the first time that we really started to go through it, first of all, we had to figure out how we would process it, because it was quite a large amount of material and it wasn't clear from the beginning that this would be something that I would be working on or whether it would be other people in the team. So again my memory is that I believe it was in May that we took a -- that there was a mission to Bosnia and that a small group of interpreters and I began to go through the photocopied material and began to enter it into an Excel table to begin to analyse the contents. After that, we started -- we developed the other database and began to work through the notebooks by data, because dates were -- there was a limited time, and particular dates were of higher priority than other dates. So it was just a gradual process of working through the material in a methodical manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, since I wanted to know when you began exactly, I believe you said May but did not mention the year.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998. It would have been earlier than that that I would have had a preliminary sort of look at the material, but that we really started to work on it I think it was May of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did other team members have access to the material or were you the only one?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Other team members also had access to the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please specify those team members provided you recall their names.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military analyst Rick Butler; Peter Nicholson, who wasn't officially on the Srebrenica team but helped in several field missions; interpreters; Jean-Rene Ruez, the team leader; Peter McCloskey, the Prosecutor. For those who didn't speak the language, of course, their ability to work with it was very -- well, it was limited. I mean, they couldn't really work with it, but they certainly had access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether there are any notes in existence about the material reviewed by you at the time, and are there any notes about the programme as you said you created at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there would have been a trip report or a couple of trip reports about the translation that we did in the field, but I don't recall any other specific notes about the -- I'm not quite sure what you mean when you refer to "programme."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you said in one of your answers that you created a project, specifying how you were to go about researching that material. I wanted to know whether there are any notes still in existence pertaining to such research about the material provided by the military service.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really came out in the form of a product [realtime transcript read in error "protect"], of an Excel table in which there was analysis and then also a database. There's a typo on the transcript. I think I said "product" and not "protect." Line 21. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Tell us this, please: After your service with the Tribunal, that is to say after 2000, did you have occasion to work with any other intercepts until you returned here in 2006 as the special advisor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain the nature of work you carried out after your employment with the Tribunal. For example, the work you did for the Prosecutor's office of the ICC.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the ICC I was responsible for helping to start the field investigations for the Darfur investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to the Chamber how you became engaged in that and how it was implemented, the work you carried out.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hired by the Prosecutor to -- because I had had experience in eastern Chad. The Prosecutor of the ICC had asked me to come on board to help them get their investigation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you specify that period, the beginning and the end of your engagement, perhaps if you remember the month and year.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: June 2005 to June 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whether at the time you worked for any NGOs, and, if so, which ones. If you indeed worked for certain NGOs during what period was that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous testimony I mentioned that I worked for the Coalition for International Justice which was a nonprofit based in Washington, DC from 2000 until 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry. Was this NGO of yours deployed to crisis areas between 2000 and 2005? What is it present in certain conflict areas?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based in Washington, DC, but sometimes it required travel to other areas. I travelled, for example, to East Timor on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your travel to East Timor related to the conflict there exclusively?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during the post-conflict situation -- or post-conflict period, but, yes, it had to do with the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the relationship between your NGOs and the globalisation process? That is to say, what is their position vis-à-vis globalisation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The NGOs you worked for, for whom you travelled to crisis areas during the crises and post-crises, the areas such as Bosnia and Chad as well as East Timor, did they send you there as part of their projects in conflict-affected areas, and was that in any way related with globalisation and the creation of the new world order?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role was very specific and had to do with -- for example, in East Timor, it was to assist the UN in setting up a special court to try the crimes that had been committed when the Indonesian military withdrew from East Timor. I just can't respond -- I don't know how to respond to your question about globalisation and the creation of the new world order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we seem to be speaking at cross-purposes concerning these particular issues, I -- I'd like to move on to the next topic. Regard -- as regards any analyses and testimony offered by you before this Tribunal in various proceedings, did you also provide a report, because most experts usually provide written statements or reports, whereas I have never seen one originated by you. Concerning the analyses you carried out, did you create a report or not? Was it simply an ad hoc exercise?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not create a report. The product was essentially the information that was summarised in an excel table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a reason why you did not carry out analyses, produce reports, or provide statements? Is there any other reason in existence in addition to your simply stating that you actually were included in it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My part of the work and those that I worked with was to analyse the material and to determine whether we considered it to be authentic or genuine and reliable. So the analysis of what the material meant was really incorporated by the military analyst into the overall case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether as an investigator or a former investigator of the OTP, were you under an obligation to protect the interests of the Prosecution when publicly presenting the results of your findings?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My obligation is to this court and to speaking the truth and providing the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is your obligation vis-a-vis the Tribunal, much as any other citizen would have, but in particular vis-a-vis the Prosecutor's office, did you have to protect their interests as a member of the same office since you were either their employee or advisor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe when I started we had to sign a document that talked about the confidentiality and retaining confidentiality with the material that we worked with, but I think that's different from your question about protecting their interests, and I'm not sure what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for stating that it wasn't sufficiently clear. I'll try to clarify. Were you under an obligation to, say, protect or guard the interests of the Prosecutor's office as stated in the indictment and other documents produced by the OTP and presented to the court while you were employed here?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, "interest" to me is an odd word to use. Maybe if you could provide the document that says that I could take a look at it, but I always felt an obligation to retain confidentiality, to retain integrity, and to be honest in the work that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to go by this in yet a different way. Can you explain in brief what were your loyalty obligations vis-a-vis the Prosecutor's office while you worked here, and are you still under such an obligation? Thank you. I apologise. I will repeat my question, because I want it reflected accurately. What loyalty obligations and protecting the Office of the Prosecutor from competition while you were working for the Prosecutor's office, and are you still under such an obligation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What competition?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I said forbidding competition, whereas something else seems to have been interpreted to you. Maybe "forbidding competitions" means something else to you, since in the meantime you seem to have been working for the NGOs, for the NGO sector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The accused may have in mind the concept of "conflict of interest," yet he's not using the words to describe that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will try to use an example. When you worked for the NGOs later on, could you use the examples presented to you at this Tribunal and its Prosecutor's office? Given the fact that you also worked for some other international courts which prosecuted parties to other conflicts, could you specifically use the data and knowledge you gained by researching the documents for this Prosecutor's office, and were you under an obligation by this OTP to keep such information confidential at that time and now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If information was not public then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since these are Military Intelligence Service information and since you said that it was valuable information, they were all secret. It was all secret. Are you still under an obligation to keep that secret now, or is there still any ban in existence in terms of forbidden competition vis-a-vis this Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a public hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We seem to be -- have a problem with the word "competition." I'm interested in this: Could you, for example, work as an expert of Defence since you seem to have been an expert for the Prosecution? Perhaps this will clarify the term "competition" or rivalry. The word in B/C/S is "konkurencija."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not here as an expert witness. Secondly, I'm aware that this court has made a decision that former members of the Prosecutor's office have been able to work both for the Defence and the Chambers. The decisions that this court makes are its own. I can't imagine taking such a decision. I don't think it applies to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any decision by this court or the Prosecutor's office that would corroborate what you just said?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I don't think it's my position to give the examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the transcript, could you tell us whether you are in possession of any decision of this Tribunal which would give you full freedom in terms of your participation in any other case, even on the side of the Defence, for example, since you used to work for the OTP? Is there any such document by the OTP which would prohibit you from working for any Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I object to the question. The witness already -- the witness has already answered it. She says as far as she's aware there's nothing that precludes her from working for the Defence, and I think that ends the issue there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last question included something additionally, if she knows a specific document, and I think the witness is able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot point to a specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The last sentence uttered by the witness was not interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The sentence was: "I cannot point to a specific document." Did you receive now the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I did, even before you repeated it, because the interpreters were lagging behind slightly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During the testimony in the cases of Blagojevic, Krstic, and Popovic, did you carry out a selection of material that was to be tendered through you or was that selection done by any OTP representatives such as Mr. Thayer or Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, just to correct the record, I didn't testify in the Blagojevic case. So with respect to Krstic and Popovic, the Prosecutors ultimately had the say in which intercepts were included in the material that was presented during the trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, whether in the team which studied the intercepts by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina there was anyone who was not a US citizen like yourself, excluding the head of team, Mr. Ruez, because he was not directly involved in this.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't understand that "yes," what it referred to. Yes, there was, or yes there wasn't? Was there anybody there who was not from the United States so that I don't have to go into the list of who else was in that team that analysed the list of the -- the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were other people involved who were -- who were not US citizens, who were Bosnian citizens, who were interpreters. Translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Can you please tell us, except for the interpreters or the translator, of course you need translators for the materials that are in the Serbian language, thank you, but was there anyone other than them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that I worked on the intercepts, there wasn't -- there weren't other investigators or team members who worked on them as closely as I did with the interpreters. We communicated a lot back and forth, the investigators, myself, the interpreters, the Prosecutor, about not only the intercepts but about new information that was coming into the investigation, but I was the primary person along with the interpreters who were working on -- who was working on this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During these proceedings in this case, we've seen that Mr. Ruez received some material. Other than receiving this material in the period when you were also receiving material, did he just receive this material or did he also conduct certain analysis of the material and is there a record of such an analysis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He just received the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So he just has that document indicating that he had received and signed for the material that is for the needs of this OTP; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than doing it in that way with Ruez establishing the contacts with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you please tell us how you established contacts with the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to obtain the intercept material? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Srebrenica investigative team, so I established contact with them in the context of all of the other team members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, you emphasise that immediately after the Srebrenica events you got in touch with the Bosnian authorities. I would like you now to explain to the Trial Chamber how you got in touch with them, in what way, and were you in the team then immediately after the conflict or again I have received an erroneous interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was with Jean-Rene Ruez and two other people when we first went to Tuzla in July of 1995. There were rumours, television broadcasts, CNN broadcasts that something had happened in Srebrenica, and the Tribunal took the initiative to send a small team to Tuzla to see whether there was any substance to those reports. We stayed -- we established contact -- Jean-Rene Ruez established contact. I was a member of that group of four. He was the primary person. He established contact with the SDB in Tuzla, and we began to review statements that the police had been collecting from people who had been streaming out of the enclave, many of them by foot. My recollection is that we stayed there for about one month. I then came back, and another team of investigators flew to Tuzla and began conducting interviews with survivors of the mass executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that in 1995 you did not establish any kind of contacts in order to obtain intercepts? I asked you when was the first time that you established contacts in order to obtain the intercepts. These were other investigative actions that you mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time in July of 1995, Jean-Rene Ruez asked the SDB whether there were intercepted communications. There were rumours that there were. As we've discussed, we weren't given access to that material until March of 1998. So in the interim period, Jean-Rene Ruez made several requests, mostly verbal, to the SDB with whom he had established a relationship, and certainly I also knew people there in the context of mostly witnesses and ongoing investigative activities, but it wasn't until the spring of 1998 that we began to receive material, intercepted communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I at this point in time put a question to the witness. Ms. Frease, could you help me. At the beginning of the examination by Mr. Tolimir this afternoon, you explained that you worked for the Tribunal, for the OTP, between 1998 and 2000. Now you're telling us that you have been in the region in 1995 already. Could you explain that to us. When did you start to work for the OTP, and what happened from the first beginning up to 1998, so that we have it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I began to work for the Tribunal in April of 1995, and my employment with the Tribunal continued until July of 2000. I think the confusion arose around when I began to work on the intercepted communication, which was in 1998. But prior to that time I had uninterrupted employment with the OTP and worked for a large portion of that time on the Srebrenica investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the period that the President asked you about, did you have any contacts with persons who had any kind of connection or anything to do with the intercepted conversations in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that I assume you mean the period from 1995 to the spring of 1998. And the answer is no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you bring anything at the time for the needs of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, meaning any kind of technical equipment or expendable material? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no contact -- I had no contact with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina until we had contact with them specifically with respect to the intercepted communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were the main bearer of that task, could you please tell us who was the person that you got in touch with first, and when did this contact take place for the first time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify that it was Jean-Rene Ruez who made a request to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't remember whether it was to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or it was to the SDB in late 1997 to have access to the radio intercepts. At that time I was not involved in the radio intercepts, and it was unclear, even when we first got the first 550 pages, that greenish-blue binder that we saw a photograph of on Wednesday, that I would be involved in the project. It was not clear from the beginning. So I think your question is slightly misstated in that I became involved in the project after it was already going. So in April I was introduced to the people that the previous team had met and established contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us when you established contact for the first time and with whom, and from which command of the B and H Army in order to obtain the radio intercepts? Was it an official contact or a private contact? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My work with the Tribunal always went through official contacts, and the contact was with the 2nd Corps. We met with -- I believe we met with the commander of the 2nd Corps at the time, and then we met with the person who was in charge of the intelligence unit at the time. I could mention names if that's necessary. I don't know whether we're doing that in this session or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These are public figures who were at that post at the time in the federation -- in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I don't see why you wouldn't be able to mention their names in these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid of getting the rank wrong, so I won't mention the rank. I'll just mention the name. Budakovic and I believe it was Colonel Sevko Tihic. From there, then, once we established the official contact at the appropriate level, then we were given access to lower-level majors and others who were actually involved in the hands-on radio communication interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to say for the transcript, without referring to names, what type of contact was established with the intelligence unit of the 2nd Corps and your team, the team of the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was professional contact. We were taken to the two sites. They explained to us what they did at those sites and in general terms how they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps we can just leave aside this situation in Tuzla and the 2nd Corps, and you can tell us whether the OTP, at the time when you were processing the radio intercepts, requested to talk with the intelligence service that was dealing with the intercepts from the United States, Great Britain, France, those intelligence services who had their presence in the theatre also where your investigators were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether any of this is confidential. We attempted to establish contact with the United States on this subject, but we didn't get very far. My recollection is that they were able to confirm a few of the code-names, Panorama, Badem, Palma, that sort of thing, but nothing more. Or maybe I should say unwilling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you need to verify the reliability of this material through some foreign intelligence services that had their electronic surveillance aircraft or troops in the area where the activity was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't able to verify the reliability through the means that you mention. However, we were able to verify the reliability in other ways, which we've discussed over the last few days. I would add that the additional information that we've received from Croatia further corroborates the material that we've been working with over the last many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you felt there was a need for purposes of reliability of some material which was incomplete or you could not verify in any other way to have other similar material either from other intelligence services that were in the area and that were present in the airwaves with their electronic listening devices? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that would have been optimal, but as you know and as we've discussed, it's -- radio intercepted communication is really highly valued and highly protected by intelligence services, so we weren't able to, at the time, get that sort of corroboration from other intelligence services. Nonetheless, we were able to authenticate the material that we did receive, and by testing it in many ways also consider it reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We talked about the reliability and authenticity and the completeness, and we will talk about this with specific documents in mind, but what I'm asking is whether it would be desirable in the work of an analyst to see this process, how it was conducted by other parties to check whether all the information is present with all sources who were doing the same kind of thing, because other users also were collecting this information. For example, NATO was overseeing the electronic surveillance, so if anyone established communications, they would monitor the communications and then they would impose no-flight bans and were recording everything. So were you able to check your material by checking with this kind of information sources? Did you try to contact anyone, you or the OTP, of those who were engaged on the monitoring of this type of material? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to hear the answer and then Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, we're getting into an area of Rule 70 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's something different. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. I apologise. We -- it's very possible we are making -- we make Rule 70 requests to many governments. As you're aware, we make Rule 70 requests on these topics, and the actual request is -- is something that, you know, I think we've gone into that and she's answered it, but any more detail than this and we may be getting into responses to such, and that is something that I -- I'm sorry to take out of turn, but I need to protect the record for because we need to protect Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the Defence aware of the conditions of this state made by your -- for your application?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given our -- our communication with the Defence is not always as thorough as it could be, I think the Defence understands the Rule 70 aspect of the aerial images because that's been a matter that has -- and I apologise to Judge Nyambe, that has been a matter that's been litigated over and over again and is part of the record, and there's been objections that have been made. And as for areas related to intercepted conversations, it's -- there is no history of that. I have not had any discussions with Mr. Gajic about that, and, frankly, I can't remember if there even is a history at this point, but it's just a sensitive area and I think it's something that we need to take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I've just got one question for Mr. McCloskey. Why you're apologising to me in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was apologising when I was -- I noticed I was talking behind the pole and looking at Judge Fluegge. So I realised that I was accidentally excising you out, so that's why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- pushed my head around the pole. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Welcome to the other side of the pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only I was in a position to see your body language, and therefore Judge Nyambe couldn't realise what you were referring to. Mr. Tolimir, I think the position of the Prosecution is quite clear. You should take into account that there might and problem for the witness if she got into an area which is related to Rule 70 material provided by another state, but please carry on and try to find out what is possible to obtain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's sufficient for us when the Prosecutor replies instead of the witness, because that is also entered into the transcript. If I put some questions to the witness that they are unable to answer but they are -- they know the answer, then I kindly ask that they request a closed session so that they can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you do you need a private or closed session in order to be able to answer some of the questions that I put to you previously? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that would not help very much because if a state or an entity made such a condition pursuant to Rule 70 not to give the information, the source or other things, then the Chamber and the Defence or anybody else in this Tribunal will not be able in the position to receive this information. This is the problem. It's not the problem of open or closed session but the problem is at all we are allowed to get this information. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's sufficient for me for the witness to say whether she is aware of any Rule 70 limitations, and if she's unable to answer the question. What is important to me is for the witness to say whether she did not or did use any other material or sources from other intelligence entities in order to verify the radio intercepts that she was working on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm convinced Ms. Frease is aware of the line she isn't allowed to pass. Therefore, please carry on with your answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1998, I believe it was the end of 1998, we tried to obtain additional information, as I mentioned before, from the United States. However, we didn't receive very much in return. In the meantime and during my present testimony, we have discussed intercepted communication that has come from Croatia and also from another source from which we heard audiotapes and transcripts. So all of this further reaffirms my confidence in the material that we received in 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is not my intention to ask for anything that I do not need in order to put my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could we please look at P787, please, in e-court. We are familiar with this document. It's already an exhibit. We can see it now. It is dated the 24th of July, 1995, sent by chief of SDB sector to the Military Security Service Department of the 2nd Corps. So they received this from him. In the transcript, page 5000, lines 5 and 20, in answer to one of the questions, you said as follows, and the question was put by

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: "In your previous testimony you said that Bosnia and Herzegovina had certain reservations or tried to refuse handing over certain material," and you answered affirmatively. She asked you why you think that they had that position. Your answer was that. "... in 1995 the war was still ongoing and intercepted radio communication is a sensitive issue. That type of intelligence information is considered a jewel in the crown. They used that material in realtime to forward it to their command posts or to protect their personnel, or they conveyed what they deemed relevant. At that time, we had still not established relations with them, and because the war was ongoing, I believe it was understandable that they were reserved and resisting the hand-over of such sensitive material to people they did not know who may leak that material, in which case their crucial interests may come in jeopardy." That was on page 5000. Do you remember saying something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are running out of time with the first session. I think we need the first break now, and we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were able to read the document. Have I correctly quoted you concerning your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document we have on the screen states that the material needs to be sent immediately. The date is the 24th July, 1995. The document is compiled by the SDB, which was authorised to contact international organisations and bodies within the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They say that materials should be forwarded to you immediately in order to have a file created. Does this reflect what you said before the Trial Chamber, or is this about something else?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't seen these documents before the Popovic trial, and what this is is a request from the Ministry of Interior, the service -- the SDB, the service that we first made contact with, and it's a request from them to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina asking the 2 Corps command to hand over radio intercepts to us. So it affirms what I said before, that we had knowledge, we had heard that they were radio intercepts. We had asked for them from the police, but we had never received them, and I didn't know until the Popovic trial that these requests had been made by the police to the military. The military made a decision not to hand over anything to us until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the transcript, can you tell us whether immediately after the events in Srebrenica, as early as July, for example the 24th of July as in this document, when I was in Zepa, there was an order requesting that intercept material be handed over to the Prosecutor's office by Bosnian authorities. Have any such orders been issued at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have this request in front of us, but as I said, I wasn't aware of any formal requests or, as you call them, orders at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You weren't aware of it, but can you tell us for the record whether they indeed received a request for the material to be handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the military received a request? I don't know. I wasn't in the military. I mean, from this document it appears that they did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Therefore, they were requested to hand over the documents to you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this done by the most senior official from the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the gentleman who signed this order was the highest authority in Tuzla from the SDB, from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that this SDB representative had free field to play on to provide you the material with a level playing field, or did he have to turn to the army for that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that he turned to the army for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But since he turned to the army, would it not have been logical for him to provide the SDB material as well in addition to the army material, because I believe you relied on SDB material as well.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, we did not receive material from the SDB until May of 1999. We did not know that the SDB was working at the same site as 2 Corps until May of 1999, until we began to interview the intercept operators. My recollection is that -- my recollection is that the explanation that was given at the time was that the SDB was intercepting communication on radio frequency 836 and that it was therefore a sort of higher-level radio intercept -- that they were higher-level radio intercepts and that the material that they thought would be more valuable was the stuff that the lower -- the material that was being intercepted on the different frequencies that the military was focusing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the last sentence. I'll quote: "We need the audio material in order to create a file which will be handed over to the International Tribunal in The Hague." What does that sentence tell us? That the SDB is asking for material to create a file which in turn was supposed to be forwarded to you. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You, as Tribunal representatives, or perhaps someone from your team, had you already sent a request to B and H organs for the hand-over of such material prior to this document, or was this done of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this would have been -- this would have had to have been done of their own accord because we had arrived in Tuzla a couple of days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When did Mr. Ruez ask for that material, and when did you get information of that material's existence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when Mr. Ruez made formal requests, RFAs, right, requests for information, regarding the radio intercepts. There is reference to a request having been made in late 1997 in which we -- my prepositions are messed up. Just a minute. And for which or as a result of which we then got access to the material in March of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you reviewed all that material, is there a document in the OTP that is being kept by the OTP that had been sent to B and H authorities requesting all material pertaining to war crimes which actually served as the basis for any ongoing discussions about the fate of such material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OTP made ongoing requests for information, so I wouldn't be able to point to just one request. It was also a procedure that was being established, the idea of requests for information, requests for assistance. In 1995, of course, the Tribunal was still quite new and was establishing its own internal procedures about how to request information from governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were the head of team concerning the intercepts and the processing of those intercepts and that you started working in 1995. Does that mean that somewhere in your archives there should be a request sent to the B and H organs, and did you ever invoke that request at a later point in time? We see on this document that it was sent in July 1995, and you say that you received SDB material as late as 1999, in May, and in 1998 you received material from the Army of B and H. Can you explain to us why the time gap?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's important to remember that Jean-Rene Ruez was the team leader and that the requests for information were mostly initiated by him and going through him and information coming back to him. I started working on the intercepts, as we've already mentioned several times, in the spring of 1998, but that I was first involved in the investigation in July of 1995. I believe we looked at a document that Jean-Rene Ruez wrote that goes through the chronology of when requests were made for the intercepts, both verbally and then in writing, and that would have been something that he would have done and that I was not responsible for doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is clear to me, but I'm asking you this: Did you as part of your file have a document in terms of requesting material that you subsequently analysed, and did you try to conclude why the material was not incoming, whereas at the same time the whole world was talking about Srebrenica and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a document would have been in the team files. I don't remember having any such specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at an e-court document. It is P788. Thank you. We can see it now in Serbian and in English. It is very brief. It is noteworthy to look at the document. It is dated 18 August 1995, and the title is: "Provision of Materials for the International Tribunal, Instruction." It was signed by Chief Brigadier General Jusuf Jasarevic who was Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He is sending this to the 2nd Corps command. He says: "We have been informed through the Sarajevo MUP SDB that in their document 7-1022 of 24 July 1995, the Tuzla SDB requested audio recordings from you regarding incidents linked with Srebrenica. Since the recordings requested are very important to the dossier being formed for the International War Crimes Tribunal it is essential that these materials be provided to the Tuzla SDB sector." Signed by chief Brigadier General Jusuf Jasarevic. We see that this was the military intelligence service administration of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question is this: Is this not another document which clearly indicates that in July and August all bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the army, the staff, and the state security service worked actively on the creation of that file and seeking material from the 2nd Corps, whereupon they did not receive that audio material which they specifically asked for? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that they worked specifically on the file. This is a document that's created by, as you said, you know, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think you need to ask them. The first time that I saw this document was also in the Popovic case. I was completely unfamiliar with the previous document and this document until -- until they were presented, I think, in the cross-examination during the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an analyst, is it clear to you that these two documents indicate that the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as early as July and August 1995, worked on the creation of the file, asking for the audio material to be received from the 2nd Corps; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm uncomfortable with the term that they "worked on creation of the file." I understand that you're taking it from the last sentence of the previous document. I mean, my understanding and my interpretation of that previous document was that the SDB at the time was trying to assist the Tribunal in providing information that would be useful in its investigation of the alleged crimes that took place in Srebrenica during the fall of the enclave. So this document -- let me backtrack. This document is a response, clearly, to the first document that you showed in which the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Main Staff, is asking 2 Corps to hand over material to the SDB in order for the SDB to hand over material to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the author of this document, Jusuf Jasarevic, referring to the document of the 24th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can go back to the first document to double-check the numbers, but certainly it refers to a document on the 24th of July. I don't remember off the top of my head whether it is -- whether that document number was 7-1022 as is indicated here. My guess is that it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you need to see it, can we please have these two documents shown to you in e-court. That would be P787 as well as this document that we're looking at now on the left-hand side. Actually, we can see it now, and we can see where it says with its document 7-1022, dated 24 of July, 1995, and then at the top in the heading we can see that same number, the 24th of July. You can see 7-1022 --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like there's also a J behind it; right? In the original document 7-1022J, maybe? Anyway, yes, the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't really matter for us to establish that. What I would like you to say is whether there was a will, because you couldn't say whether you know or don't know, but was there a will among the state security organs and the military security organs to provide the materials to the Tribunal? Yes or no? Thank you. Can that be seen on the basis of these documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since there was a will both on the part of the State Security Service as well as the intelligence security organs of the B and H Army, can you please then say why this material was not provided to you until 1998 and May 1999, as you mentioned a little bit earlier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think this question has been put to the witness already on a number of occasions. She's already answered it, and I don't see that we're getting anywhere by re-putting the question to the witness on the basis of this document or any other document. She referred specifically to the note that -- that was prepared by Mr. Ruez in relation to requests that were made and in relation to the responses that were had as a result -- in relation to this material, and I don't know that asking the question again is going to produce a different answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to hear the answer, maybe very brief, but without any further repetitions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why this material was not produced earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you it. Carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, it's very important for you to clearly state for the transcript whether you know why did you establish that in your analysis, why you did not receive these documents at the time this initiative was started by the organs that you requested the documents from, why did it take three years for this to happen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now I think this is really a repetition. The witness stated several times that she was involved analysing this material in 1998 and not earlier and was not responsible for that, and especially about the reasons why the -- the army and the MUP in Bosnia was not responding earlier, she says very clearly she doesn't know, and therefore I think it's not the appropriate witness to -- to maintain this information. You should perhaps wait for another witness who could help you with this information. Please, not again the same question, but carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thought that this witness knew why it did not receive something that was requested and that initiative was launched to receive this document, so in the beginning I quoted what the witness thinks why this material was not handed over, but the witness said that they were willing. There was a will for them to hand it over. This is what I am trying to show. If you have something, you hand it over. If you don't, then you are not able to hand it over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This witness was not working for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina but for the Prosecutor's office, and she said very clearly several times that she doesn't know. I think you should leave it like it is and move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now we're going to look at Exhibit P789, if possible. Can we look at it in e-court. We will not force the witness to say anything. It's enough for her to say yes or no. I mean that constitutes an answer as far as I'm concerned. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see up on the screen a document of the 2nd Corps command, the security department that had this material, these radio intercepts, in their possession. The document speaks about all initial documents, requesting them to hand over the audio material. And if you can look in the second paragraph of the document, they say: "In accordance with the above, we request that you make a selection among your audio recordings relating to the fall of Srebrenica which contain data relating to war crimes and the crimes of genocide by the aggressor against the inhabitants of the so-called 'safe area.' We request that you submit this to us so that we can forward it to the Tuzla CSB - SDB Tuzla in compliance with the above requests." So you can see that this date, actually this document was sent as early as August, and that in the last sentence it states: "We request that you act upon with this document as soon as possible in order for us to fulfil the aforementioned tasks in a timely fashion." My question is: As an analyst, did you take note of this second paragraph where a selection of audio material is being requested? What does this selection mean according to you? What is that supposed to refer to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also saw this document for the first time during the Popovic trial, and I guess my answer in part is the same, that I'm not sure I'm the right person to -- to be asking this to. In 1998, it's true that we received a selection of material in that blue binder, those 550 pages. It could be that that's the kind of selection that they're referring to here, but again it -- I'm not a member of the -- haven't ever been a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so I'm not exactly sure what that means, but it could -- it could mean something like what I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were investigator relating to the materials that were provided to you. As an investigator, did you ask yourself whether a selection was given to you of material that the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army felt the Prosecution should or shouldn't know, and could that be the outcome, and could that affect the reliability of this document in view of this collection of documents, in view of the fact that a selection was made as to what would be included or not in the binder? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We took that very seriously, and that was why it was so important that we receive the notebooks, all of the notebooks, and that we with be allowed to go through them thoroughly, from cover to cover, conversation to conversation. It was also the reason that it was important for us to receive all of the electronic versions of the conversations, so that we felt that we were getting a complete record of what had been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We also saw the last time at the end that these electronic transcripts or records were incomplete. Does this, too, raise some doubts about the material having been processed in a -- in an appropriate way suiting the interests of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then in turn presented to you as material that you requested? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notebooks were certainly complete. That's something that I can talk about because I worked on those for a long period of time. The electronic records came later for me. I cannot say with a hundred per cent certainty that we received all of them. I believe that we did, but I would need to review the files completely to be able to give you a thorough answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have looked at these three documents of the B and H Army that we pulled up on the screen and which you seen before in an earlier trial, and you can see that there was a will among all the organs to provide these documents, but still you did not receive them? What I'm asking you now is this: Did you inquire about the technical and personnel resources at the disposal of the SDB? For example, did they have an audio-recording lab, and how much time did they need in order to make this selection of material? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's -- I'd like you to clarify your question a little bit because there are a couple of different issues inside of it. One of them has to do with the material that was provided by the military, by the army, and the other is a question about the SDB. So could you break your question down for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The army provided you with material in 1998, as you stated in your previous testimony, and the MUP provided material to you in May 1999; is this correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you can see by the documents that we just looked at that the MUP was actually supposed to provide this material to you and take it from the army, because they were given the assignment of compiling and putting together this audio material. It talks about audio material. So I'm asking you whether you know what the equipment and personnel resources were at the disposal of the State Security Service. Did they have an audio lab in this period when the request for material was submitted to the time when the material was actually submitted to you in 1998 and 1999? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the SDB was working from the northern site during the time in question. I do not know about their lab facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If necessary, I can break down my question even further, but here is a sub-question: Do you know what the duties of the State Security Service are and what kind of assignments or jobs does it carry out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in great detail, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see from these three documents that the army was supposed to provide the State Security Service with the material that is referred to here as audio recordings or radio intercepts by name? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it evident from these three documents that the army did that, that it acted pursuant to the request and handed this material over to the MUP? Is that clear from these three documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you noted that the military commander -- commanders was asking the corps command to hand over this material to the State Security Service? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you noted from the documents that the State Security Service is asking for the same thing so that we would be able to form a dossier or a file? I think I read that sentence to you earlier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you look into how much of the material was in the possession of the SDB that they used to form this dossier, and why did they then give it back to the army, and why was it the army that handed this material over to you and not the SDB, which was supposed to hand it over to you? So my question is why did the State Security Service deviate from that last sentence and return the material to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina handed this material over to you instead of the SDB? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'd like to hear the answer, because I'm pretty sure that this witness is able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually wanted to call your attention to something in the documents that we looked at yesterday, and this goes to the question. The -- at the first site, at the northern site, the SDB and the military shared information. So the SDB would provide its information to the military, and the military would then forward it to its command. The SDB also forwarded it to -- forwarded its own information to its own command. Now, my memory is a little hazy on the information that the -- I believe that there was a complete exchange of information between these two bodies. So what you will see in, for example, tab 4 or tab 5 of that binder that we looked at Wednesday afternoon, is that the heading on it says "Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina 2 Corps," but the actual agency that recorded the conversation was the SDB in Tuzla. I believe that the answer that we got when we asked this question was that the SDB felt that it was because a lot of the material was not their own that they did not have the right to hand over military intercepts to the OTP without the military's consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen in the document P788 that the Brigadier General, the chief, Jusuf Jasarevic, agreed. He gave the permission for the military documents to be handed over to the state security. We saw that in the document. And we've also seen in the first document that the state security said that they were the ones to form the dossier was supposed to be handed over. I read to you the last sentence which was quite important. And we saw from your answer now that the DB had this material. So there was a request for something that they already had. Now, please tell me why did the DB hand you over this material in May 1999 and why did the army provide you with their material in 1998, and in these three years, from 1995 to 1998, was the material being processed perhaps by the state security, if they had a lab or something like that? Thank you. Did you look into that particular question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I'm on my feet again and the reason is because in this last question there are about five questions. One is why did the state security agency act one way, why did the army act another way, why didn't they turn the information over immediately. And I think it would be more helpful and perhaps more efficient if Mr. Tolimir could put his questions one at a time to the witness so that she can fairly understand them and answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness asked earlier for a break-up of a long and detailed question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, though, to this last series of questions, really, I don't feel as if I'm the right person to answer the question, because I didn't work -- I -- I was outside of this whole process, and I don't know the answer to the question. I don't know why it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to say why this didn't happen. I'm asking you whether you looked into the matter of these materials not being handed to you for three years, and did you look into that and could that perhaps reflect on the reliability and the authenticity of the material? Did you investigate that? I'm not asking you to answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only learned about these documents during the Popovic trial when I was in -- on cross-examination. So the answer is no, I didn't look into them because I didn't even know that the documents existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an investigator with a priority of dealing with documents that are authentic and reliable, can you please say whether the actions of the B and H authorities regarding this recorded material gives rise to any kind of doubts that something was done with that material since it was not handed over to you immediately, because it took three years before the material was actually handed over to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your point. Having been through the material as much as I have been, I do not have any doubt about the authenticity and the reliability of the material.
